# Recovering the truth: a simulated experiment {#sec-quickstart}

```{r}
#| label: sim-setup
library(sconjoint)
house <- "#004a8c"
truth <- simconjoint_truth$population
tv <- function(name) truth$value[truth$name == name]
t_start <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]]
```

Suppose 800 people each choose between two candidates ten times. We wrote down every person's
tastes before they chose, so we know, for example, that
`r round(100 * tv("share: prefer Republican"), 1)`% of the population prefers a Republican
candidate to an otherwise identical Democrat, and that long experience raises a candidate's chance
of being chosen by `r round(100 * tv("AME: long vs no experience"), 1)` percentage points on
average. This chapter runs the whole workflow on those choices and checks whether the estimates
land on those numbers.

The data are the package's `simconjoint`. The chapter runs live, every step from the raw choices.
It uses a small network and modest integration rules, so it finishes in about five minutes on a
recent laptop; most of that time is the three fits. The paper's settings are larger and slower,
and they would give somewhat tighter answers, but every step is the same.

## The experiment

Each candidate has four attributes: party, experience, policy position and gender. The levels are
drawn at random, each attribute on its own, as in most conjoint experiments. The data hold one row
per candidate, two rows per task:

```{r}
#| label: sim-data
head(simconjoint, 4)
```

In the first task, respondent 1 saw a moderate Democrat with some experience on the left and a
liberal Republican with some experience on the right, both men, and chose the Democrat. Every
respondent also has
three characteristics: age, ideology on a seven-point scale from $-3$ (very liberal) to 3 (very
conservative), and gender.

`sc_design()` describes how the experiment drew the candidates. It also fixes how a candidate
becomes numbers: each attribute gets one 0/1 indicator per level other than its first, six coded
features in all. `sc_code()` turns the two candidates of each task into their difference, first
minus second.

```{r}
#| label: sim-design
des <- sc_design(list(party = c("Democrat", "Republican"),
                      experience = c("none", "some", "long"),
                      position = c("liberal", "moderate", "conservative"),
                      gender = c("male", "female")), tasks = 10)
des
A <- simconjoint[simconjoint$profile == 1, ]          # first (left) candidate of each task
B <- simconjoint[simconjoint$profile == 2, ]
X <- sc_code(des, A, B)
head(X, 3)
```

`sc_data()` collects the choices (1 when the first candidate was chosen), the coded differences,
the respondent ids, and the respondent characteristics that will predict mean tastes. Passing the
design lets `sc_states()` later average over the comparisons each respondent could have seen.

```{r}
#| label: sim-scdata
Z <- as.matrix(A[!duplicated(A$id), c("age", "ideology", "female")])
rownames(Z) <- unique(A$id)
x <- sc_data(A$chosen, X, A$id, Z = Z, groups = data.frame(female = Z[, "female"]), design = des,
             orientation = "y = 1 selects the first (left) candidate; X = first minus second")
x
```

## The truth

The choices follow the package's model exactly (@sec-intro). Respondent $i$ has tastes
$\beta_i = \mu(Z_i) + \Lambda u_i$ with two taste factors, and a persistent pull
$a_i = \sqrt{\omega}\, v_i$ toward the left candidate on top of the average pull $\kappa$. The
mean tastes $\mu(Z)$ bend with the respondent's characteristics. The taste for a Republican
rises with ideology and flattens out for strong partisans. Older respondents value experience
more, and policy tastes follow a loss around the respondent's own position. The first taste factor
moves party and policy together; the second moves experience and gender. The help page
`?simconjoint` gives every formula. Here $\kappa = 0.2$ and $\omega = 0.3$.

```{r}
#| label: sim-truth
simconjoint_truth$parameters[c("kappa", "omega")]
simconjoint_truth$parameters$loading
```

The population values the chapter estimates are in `simconjoint_truth$population`. The
characteristics take a finite number of values, so each value is an exact sum over them, with
integrals inside computed by quadrature to about $10^{-6}$ or better.

## Fits with one, two and three taste factors

`sc_fit()` splits the respondents into five folds and fits the model once per fold, each time on
the other four. We fit with one, two and three taste factors. The settings are small: a network
with one hidden layer of 8 units, one start, at most 100 epochs, and Sobol rules of 128 to 256
nodes.

```{r}
#| label: sim-fit
small <- list(hidden = 8L, seeds = 1L, control = list(max_epochs = 100L, patience = 5L),
              nodes = 128L, check_nodes = 256L, heldout_nodes = 256L, verbose = FALSE)
t0 <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]]
fits <- lapply(1:3, function(q) do.call(sc_fit, c(list(x, q = q), small)))
t_fit <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]] - t0
```

## The number of taste factors

`sc_select_rank()` scores each fit on the respondents it did not train on. It moves from $q - 1$
to $q$ factors only when the gain in held-out log score is more than two standard errors.

```{r}
#| label: sim-rank
rank <- sc_select_rank(fits)
rank
fit <- fits[[which(rank$selected)]]
```

```{r}
#| label: sim-rank-text
#| echo: false
q_sel <- rank$q[rank$selected]
```

The rule picks $q = `r q_sel`$`r if (q_sel == 2) ", the true number" else ", not the true number, 2"`. The second
factor improves the held-out score by `r round(rank$z[2], 1)` standard errors; the third changes it
by `r round(rank$z[3], 1)`, which is noise. Two factors are needed because respondents who share
the same characteristics still differ in two separate ways: how strongly partisan they are, and how
much they care about experience and gender.

## Fold states

`sc_states()` computes what the estimator needs from each fold's fit. The slow part is each
held-out respondent's information, an average over task sets drawn from the design. Because `x`
carries `des`, the draws follow this experiment's own randomization. We use 40 draws per
respondent; the paper used 250 to 300.

```{r}
#| label: sim-states
t0 <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]]
st <- sc_states(fit, M = 40L, ny = 4L, info_nodes = 256L, score_nodes = 512L)
t_states <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]] - t0
st
```

## Estimates against the truth

Each target names one population quantity. The contrasts are coded features, or named vectors of
them. The compensating share asks how many respondents would take a Republican with no experience
over a Democrat with long experience: for them, party outweighs experience. The contest compares a
moderate Republican woman with long experience to a liberal Democrat man with some experience,
with position effects set to zero. `sc_ame_switch()` takes its contexts from the design, and
`sc_importance(des)` uses the design's attributes as groups.

```{r}
#| label: sim-estimate
contest <- sc_code(des, data.frame(party = "Republican", experience = "long", position = "moderate", gender = "female"),
                   data.frame(party = "Democrat", experience = "some", position = "liberal", gender = "male"))
targets <- list(
  sc_mean("mean: Republican", "party_Republican"),
  sc_mean("mean: long experience", "experience_long"),
  sc_mean("mean: conservative position", "position_conservative"),
  sc_mean("mean: female candidate", "gender_female"),
  sc_share("share: prefer Republican", "party_Republican"),
  sc_share("share: prefer long experience", "experience_long"),
  sc_share("share: prefer female candidate", "gender_female"),
  sc_share("share: Republican without experience over Democrat with long",
           c(party_Republican = 1, experience_long = -1)),
  sc_contest("contest: A beats B", drop(contest)),
  sc_ame_switch("AME: long vs no experience", "experience", level = "long", ref = "none"),
  sc_importance(des, names = paste("importance:", names(des$attributes))))
t0 <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]]
est <- sc_estimate(st, targets)
t_est <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]] - t0
est$truth <- truth$value[match(est$name, truth$name)]
est$covered <- est$truth >= est$lower & est$truth <= est$upper
knitr::kable(est[, c("name", "truth", "estimate", "lower", "upper", "covered")], digits = 3,
             col.names = c("Quantity", "Truth", "Estimate", "95% lower", "95% upper", "Covered"))
```

```{r}
#| label: sim-cover
#| echo: false
n_int <- sum(!is.na(est$covered)); n_cov <- sum(est$covered, na.rm = TRUE)
miss <- est$name[which(!est$covered)]
imp <- which(est$kind == "importance"); imp_worst <- imp[which.max(abs(est$estimate[imp] - est$truth[imp]))]
imp_err <- abs(est$estimate[imp_worst] - est$truth[imp_worst])
resp <- simconjoint_truth$respondents; law <- simconjoint_truth$covariate_law
cons_sample <- mean(resp$ideology > 0); cons_pop <- sum(law$ideology_probs[law$ideology > 0])
party_sample <- mean(simconjoint_truth$beta[, "party_Republican"])
r_party <- est[est$name == "mean: Republican", ]
```

`r n_cov` of the `r n_int` intervals cover the truth`r if (length(miss)) paste0("; the miss", if (length(miss) > 1) "es are " else " is ", paste0("\"", miss, "\"", collapse = ", ")) else ""`.
With 95% intervals we expect about one miss in twenty, so one run cannot show that the coverage
is exactly right. The intervals describe the population, not these 800 people, and this sample
happens to lean right. It holds more conservatives than the population (`r round(100 * cons_sample)`%
against `r round(100 * cons_pop)`%), and its respondents' true average taste for a Republican is
`r round(party_sample, 2)`, against `r round(r_party$truth, 2)` in the population. The interval for
that mean, from `r round(r_party$lower, 2)` to `r round(r_party$upper, 2)`,
`r if (isTRUE(r_party$covered)) "covers the population value" else "covers the sample's value but not the population's"`.
The figure below puts each estimate and its interval next to the truth.

```{r}
#| label: fig-sim-estimates
#| fig-cap: "Estimates and 95% intervals (blue) against the truth (open circles)"
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.6
short <- c("Republican", "Long experience", "Conservative position", "Female candidate",
           "Prefer Republican", "Prefer long experience", "Prefer female candidate",
           "Rep., no exp., over Dem., long exp.", "Contest: A beats B", "AME: long experience",
           paste("Importance:", names(des$attributes)))
panel <- function(rows, xlab, xlim) {
  k <- length(rows); yy <- rev(seq_len(k))
  plot(NA, xlim = xlim, ylim = c(0.5, k + 0.5), yaxt = "n", xlab = xlab, ylab = "")
  abline(h = yy, col = "grey92")
  axis(2, at = yy, labels = short[rows], las = 1, tick = FALSE, cex.axis = 0.85)
  ok <- !is.na(est$lower[rows])
  segments(est$lower[rows][ok], yy[ok], est$upper[rows][ok], yy[ok], col = house, lwd = 2)
  points(est$estimate[rows], yy, pch = 19, col = house, cex = 0.9)
  points(est$truth[rows], yy, pch = 1, col = "black", cex = 1.3)
}
op <- par(oma = c(2, 0, 0, 0), cex = 0.85)
layout(matrix(1:2, 1), widths = c(1, 1.3))
par(mar = c(4.2, 9.5, 1, 0.8))
panel(1:4, "Mean taste (logit scale)", c(-0.3, 0.9))
abline(v = 0, lty = 3, col = "grey50")
par(mar = c(4.2, 13, 1, 0.8))
panel(5:14, "Share or probability", c(0, 0.85))
par(fig = c(0, 1, 0, 1), oma = c(0, 0, 0, 0), mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0), new = TRUE)
plot.new()
legend("bottom", horiz = TRUE, bty = "n", pch = c(19, 1), col = c(house, "black"), lwd = c(2, NA),
       pt.cex = c(0.9, 1.3), legend = c("Estimate and 95% interval", "Truth"))
par(op)
```

The left panel shows mean tastes on the logit scale; the right panel shows shares, probabilities,
the AME and the importance shares. Importance shares have no intervals: the package reports point
estimates for them. In this run the largest miss is `r round(100 * imp_err, 1)` points, for
`r sub("importance: ", "", est$name[imp_worst])`, so read them as rough.

In the population, two of the mean tastes are close to zero: the average respondent barely prefers
either party or either end of the policy scale. That does not mean respondents do not care. The
next figure shows why.

## The distribution of tastes

`sc_fitted_law()` gives, for each held-out respondent, the fitted normal law of a taste: mean
$c^\top\mu(Z_i)$ and standard deviation $\lVert\Lambda^\top c\rVert$. Their mixture is the
fitted population distribution. The true distribution is the same mixture with the true $\mu$ and
$\Lambda$.

```{r}
#| label: fig-sim-laws
#| fig-cap: "Fitted (blue, dashed) and true (black) distributions of two tastes"
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.8
L0 <- simconjoint_truth$parameters$loading; mu0 <- simconjoint_truth$mu
law_density <- function(m, s, grid) rowMeans(outer(grid, m, function(g, mm) dnorm(g, mm, s)))
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.2, 4.2, 1, 0.8), oma = c(2, 0, 0, 0), cex = 0.85)
for (f in c("party_Republican", "experience_long")) {
  fl <- sc_fitted_law(st, f)
  grid <- seq(-3.5, 3.5, length.out = 400)
  dt <- law_density(mu0[, f], sqrt(sum(L0[f, ]^2)), grid)
  df <- rowMeans(outer(grid, seq_len(nrow(fl)), function(g, i) dnorm(g, fl$mean[i], fl$sd[i])))
  plot(grid, dt, type = "l", lwd = 2, ylim = c(0, max(dt, df) * 1.08),
       xlab = sprintf("Taste for %s (logit scale)", c(party_Republican = "a Republican",
                                                       experience_long = "long experience")[f]),
       ylab = "Density", main = "")
  lines(grid, df, lwd = 2, col = house, lty = 2)
  abline(v = 0, lty = 3, col = "grey50")
}
par(fig = c(0, 1, 0, 1), oma = c(0, 0, 0, 0), mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0), new = TRUE)
plot.new()
legend("bottom", horiz = TRUE, bty = "n", lwd = 2, lty = c(1, 2), col = c("black", house),
       legend = c("True distribution", "Fitted distribution"))
par(op)
```

The true taste for a Republican has two humps: liberals dislike Republicans, conservatives like
them, and moderates sit in between. An average near zero hides both camps. The fitted distribution
has the right width, from about $-3$ to $3$, but it blurs the two humps into a plateau. The
network with 8 hidden units learns a mean taste that rises almost in a straight line with ideology,
while the truth, $2 \tanh(3s)$ with $s$ the ideology divided by 3, levels off for anyone left or
right of the centre. The fit makes up for the missing camps with a larger spread around the mean
(the next table). In our trials, a network with two hidden layers (16 and 8 units) found the humps
but predicted held-out choices worse, so the held-out score, which is how one would choose between
them, prefers the smoother fit. The shares and
the means are still right, because they depend on the distribution only through how much of it lies
above zero and where its centre is. The taste for long experience has one hump, recovered almost
exactly, with about three quarters of it above zero.

The loading $\Lambda$ itself is not identified: any rotation of its columns gives the same model.
What is identified is the spread of tastes among respondents who share the same characteristics,
$\Lambda\Lambda^\top$. Its diagonal gives the standard deviation of each taste among respondents
with the same characteristics. Averaged over the five folds:

```{r}
#| label: sim-spread
sd_fit <- rowMeans(sapply(st$folds, function(f) sqrt(rowSums(as.matrix(f$th$loading)^2))))
spread <- data.frame(feature = des$features, true_sd = round(sqrt(rowSums(L0^2)), 2),
                     fitted_sd = round(sd_fit, 2), row.names = NULL)
spread
```

```{r}
#| label: sim-spread-text
#| echo: false
gap <- abs(spread$fitted_sd - spread$true_sd); j <- which.max(gap)
```

The fitted spread is within `r round(max(gap[-j]), 2)` of the truth for five of the six features.
The exception is `r spread$feature[j]` (`r spread$fitted_sd[j]` against `r spread$true_sd[j]`),
where the spread absorbs the part of the mean taste the network did not learn.

## Individual respondents

`sc_posterior()` combines the fitted law with a respondent's own choices. Each respondent is
summarized at the fold that did not train on them. With no choices the posterior mean is the
fitted mean taste $\mu(Z_i)$; each choice moves it toward the respondent's own taste. `history`
sets how many of the first tasks to use, so we can watch the posterior improve as tasks accumulate.

```{r}
#| label: sim-posterior
b_true <- simconjoint_truth$beta[, "party_Republican"]
post <- lapply(c(0, 2, 5, 10), function(h)
  sc_posterior(st, contrasts = c(party_Republican = 1), history = h, nodes = 1024)$contrasts)
data.frame(tasks_used = c(0, 2, 5, 10),
           correlation = round(sapply(post, function(p) cor(p$mean, b_true)), 3),
           rmse = round(sapply(post, function(p) sqrt(mean((p$mean - b_true)^2))), 3))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-sim-posterior
#| fig-cap: "Posterior mean taste for a Republican against each respondent's true taste"
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.6
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.2, 4.2, 2, 0.8), cex = 0.85)
for (j in c(1, 4)) {
  plot(b_true, post[[j]]$mean, pch = 1, cex = 0.5, col = adjustcolor(house, 0.6),
       xlim = c(-4, 4), ylim = c(-4, 4), xlab = "True taste for a Republican",
       ylab = "Posterior mean", main = c("No tasks used", "", "", "All 10 tasks")[j], font.main = 1)
  abline(0, 1, lty = 2, col = "grey40")
  legend("topleft", bty = "n", legend = sprintf("Corr = %.2f", cor(post[[j]]$mean, b_true)))
}
par(op)
```

With no tasks, the posterior mean is the fitted $\mu(Z_i)$. It already tracks the true taste,
because ideology explains much of party taste. Ten tasks pull the posterior means closer to the
truth, and the correlation rises from `r round(cor(post[[1]]$mean, b_true), 2)` to
`r round(cor(post[[4]]$mean, b_true), 2)`. The bands of the left panel, one per ideology value,
spread out as each respondent's own choices move them, but the points still scatter widely around
the diagonal: ten choices carry limited information, and the posterior pulls each respondent toward
$\mu(Z_i)$. So the posterior is a prediction of a respondent's taste, not a measurement of it.
Population questions, such as how many prefer a Republican, should use the population targets
above, not counts of posterior means.

## What is and is not recovered

- **Recovered:** the number of taste factors; mean tastes, shares, the compensating share, the
  contest probability and the AME, with `r n_cov` of `r n_int` intervals covering the population
  value; the distribution of the taste for experience; the spread of most tastes; the position
  effects $\kappa$ and $\omega$ (each fold's values are in `summary(fit)`).
- **Recovered roughly:** importance shares, which come without intervals and miss here by up to
  `r round(100 * imp_err, 1)` points; the distribution of the taste for a Republican, whose width
  is right but whose two humps are blurred into one plateau.
- **Not recovered:** the loading $\Lambda$ itself, which is identified only up to rotation; and
  individual tastes, which ten tasks pin down only partly.

```{r}
#| label: sim-time
#| echo: false
t_total <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]] - t_start
```

This chapter took `r round(t_total / 60, 1)` minutes to run: `r round(t_fit / 60, 1)` for the
three fits, `r round(t_states / 60, 1)` for the fold states and `r round(t_est / 60, 1)` for the
estimates.

## What to try next

@sec-gs and @sec-br apply the same steps to the paper's data, starting from saved fits.
@sec-quantities lists every target. For another experiment with independently drawn attributes,
describe it with `sc_design()` and code its profiles with `sc_code()`; every step above then works
unchanged.
